claim: A 5 s optogenetic pulse of fictive carbon dioxide induced a persistent behavioral state in female mosquitoes that lasted for more than 10 min.
source: Here, we show that a 5 s optogenetic pulse of fictive carbon dioxide induced a persistent behavioral state in female mosquitoes that lasted for more than 10 min.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-D showing behavioral responses lasting over 10 minutes.

claim: The persistent behavioral state induced by fictive CO2 is highly specific to females searching for a blood meal.
source: This state is highly specific to females searching for a blood meal and was not induced in recently blood-fed females or in males, who do not feed on blood.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 3A-E showing that blood-fed females and males lack sustained responses to fictive CO2.

claim: The persistent behavioral state was not induced in recently blood-fed females.
source: This state is highly specific to females searching for a blood meal and was not induced in recently blood-fed females or in males, who do not feed on blood.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 3B showing blood-fed females completely lost their response to fictive CO2.

claim: The persistent behavioral state was not induced in males.
source: This state is highly specific to females searching for a blood meal and was not induced in recently blood-fed females or in males, who do not feed on blood.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 3C showing males had brief responses to fictive CO2 that decayed rapidly back to baseline.

claim: In males lacking the fruitless gene, fictive carbon dioxide induced a long-lasting behavior response resembling the predatory state of females.
source: In males that lack the gene fruitless, which controls persistent social behaviors in other insects, fictive carbon dioxide induced a long-lasting behavior response resembling the predatory state of females.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 3H-J showing fruitless mutant males had sustained responses to fictive CO2.

claim: The persistent state triggered by detection of fictive carbon dioxide enabled females to engorge on a blood meal mimic offered up to 14 min after the initial 5 s stimulus.
source: Finally, we show that the persistent state triggered by detection of fictive carbon dioxide enabled females to engorge on a blood meal mimic offered up to 14 min after the initial 5 s stimulus.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 4J showing females fed when the blood meal mimic was heated up to 14 minutes after fictive CO2 stimulus.

claim: Carbon dioxide produced by human breath is highly volatile, traveling long distances from the human host.
source: Carbon dioxide (CO2) produced by human breath is highly volatile, traveling long distances from the human host.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about the physical properties of CO2 and its dispersal in air.

claim: Detection of CO2 by the mosquito results in an increase in flying behavior.
source: Detection of CO2 by the mosquito results in an increase in flying behavior (Eiras and Jepson, 1991; McMeniman et al., 2014) and upwind flight (Dekker and Cardé, 2011; Dekker et al., 2005; Geier et al., 1999) that is often referred to as 'activation'.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Detection of CO2 by the mosquito results in upwind flight.
source: Detection of CO2 by the mosquito results in an increase in flying behavior (Eiras and Jepson, 1991; McMeniman et al., 2014) and upwind flight (Dekker and Cardé, 2011; Dekker et al., 2005; Geier et al., 1999) that is often referred to as 'activation'.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Mosquitoes require an additional, more proximal host cue such as body heat or skin odor for short-range attraction and to engorge on blood.
source: Mosquitoes require an additional, more proximal host cue such as body heat or skin odor for short-range attraction and to engorge on blood (Corfas and Vosshall, 2015; Dekker and Cardé, 2011; Dekker et al., 2005; Geier et al., 1999; McMeniman et al., 2014; van Breugel et al., 2015; Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Human sensory cues are typically brief and intermittent by the time they reach the mosquito due to turbulent air flows and long distances.
source: In natural settings, human sensory cues are typically brief and intermittent by the time they reach the mosquito due to turbulent air flows and long distances (Koehl, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: Studies of insect navigation have documented only short-term responses to stimuli on the order of a few seconds.
source: However, studies of insect navigation have documented only short-term responses to these stimuli on the order of a few seconds (Alvarez-Salvado et al., 2018; Dekker and Cardé, 2011; Demir et al., 2020; Pang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: The short-term role of CO2 in mosquito behavior has been known for nearly 100 years.
source: Although the short-term role of CO2 in mosquito behavior has been known for nearly 100 years (Rudolfs, 1922), the idea that CO2 induces a long-term change in the internal state of the mosquito has not previously been tested experimentally.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a 1922 publication.

claim: The idea that CO2 induces a long-term change in the internal state of the mosquito has not previously been tested experimentally.
source: Although the short-term role of CO2 in mosquito behavior has been known for nearly 100 years (Rudolfs, 1922), the idea that CO2 induces a long-term change in the internal state of the mosquito has not previously been tested experimentally.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' assessment of the prior literature.

claim: CsChrimson-tdTomato was detected in maxillary palp neurons but not antennal neurons.
source: CsChrimson-tdTomato was detected in maxillary palp neurons but not antennal neurons, consistent with the observation that maxillary palp neurons are exquisitely sensitive to CO2 (Grant et al., 1995; Figure 1C and D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1C and D, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Maxillary palp neurons are exquisitely sensitive to CO2.
source: CsChrimson-tdTomato was detected in maxillary palp neurons but not antennal neurons, consistent with the observation that maxillary palp neurons are exquisitely sensitive to CO2 (Grant et al., 1995; Figure 1C and D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: CsChrimson-expressing neurons extended axons that innervated glomerulus MD1 in the antennal lobe of the mosquito brain.
source: As expected, we found that CsChrimson-expressing neurons extended axons that innervated glomerulus MD1 in the antennal lobe of the mosquito brain (Figure 1E), which is known to be CO2-sensitive (Younger et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Glomerulus MD1 in the antennal lobe of the mosquito brain is known to be CO2-sensitive.
source: As expected, we found that CsChrimson-expressing neurons extended axons that innervated glomerulus MD1 in the antennal lobe of the mosquito brain (Figure 1E), which is known to be CO2-sensitive (Younger et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: Control animals carrying only the Gr3-QF2 driver or the QUAS-CsChrimson transgene reporter showed no response to red light.
source: Control animals carrying only the Gr3-QF2 driver or the QUAS-CsChrimson transgene reporter showed no response to red light.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Mosquitoes with both Gr3-QF2 and QUAS-CsChrimson genetic elements increased their velocity in response to red light stimulus.
source: However, mosquitoes with both genetic elements (Gr3 > CsChrimson) increased their velocity in response to the stimulus (Figure 1H–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H-I.

claim: The proportion of mosquitoes responding to optogenetic stimulation increased with light intensity.
source: The proportion of mosquitoes responding increased with light intensity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-D.

claim: When combined with another host cue such as heat, CO2 is sufficient to elicit blood feeding in female mosquitoes.
source: When combined with another host cue such as heat, CO2 is sufficient to elicit blood feeding in female mosquitoes (McMeniman et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: Control mosquitoes with either Gr3-QF2 or QUAS-CsChrimson were attracted to the warm blood meal and engorged only when presented with CO2 but not when presented with red light.
source: Control mosquitoes with either Gr3-QF2 or QUAS-CsChrimson were attracted to the warm blood meal and engorged only when presented with CO2 but not when presented with red light (Figure 1K–M).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1K-M.

claim: Gr3 > CsChrimson mosquitoes were attracted and engorged in the presence of either real or fictive CO2.
source: In contrast, Gr3 > CsChrimson mosquitoes were attracted and engorged in the presence of either real or fictive CO2, the latter delivered as a red light stimulus (Figure 1K–M).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1K-M.

claim: Mosquitoes interpreted optogenetic activation of the CO2 sensory neurons as a host cue that is sufficient to drive blood feeding.
source: These results demonstrate that mosquitoes interpreted optogenetic activation of the CO2 sensory neurons as a host cue that is sufficient to drive blood feeding.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the experimental results shown in Figure 1K-M.

claim: Host seeking begins when female mosquitoes detect a human, typically by sensing volatile cues like CO2.
source: Host seeking begins when female mosquitoes detect a human, typically by sensing volatile cues like CO2.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about mosquito behavior.

claim: Once activated by human odorants, mosquitoes seek out the source of the cues, and upon landing, mosquitoes walk to locate a patch of skin to pierce.
source: Once activated by human odorants, they seek out the source of the cues, and upon landing, mosquitoes walk to locate a patch of skin to pierce (Liu and Vosshall, 2019; McMeniman et al., 2014; van Breugel et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Delivery and removal of real CO2 necessitates constant air flow, which is itself an important sensory cue for insects.
source: Delivery and removal of real CO2 necessitates constant air flow, which is itself an important sensory cue for insects (Alvarez-Salvado et al., 2018; Kadakia et al., 2021; Suver et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: All behavior classifiers showed high accuracy with >90% true positive and true negative rates on a set of test video frames.
source: All classifiers showed high accuracy with >90% true positive and true negative rates on a set of test video frames (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 2—source data 1.

claim: Mosquitoes responded to individual heat and fictive CO2 stimuli with elevated walking, flying, and probing.
source: Mosquitoes responded to individual heat and fictive CO2 stimuli with elevated walking, flying, and probing (Figure 2E–H, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E-H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The response to heat alone was dominated by probing and returned to baseline after about 1 min.
source: The response to heat alone was dominated by probing and returned to baseline after about 1 min (t1/2 probing = 0.4 min).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Fictive CO2 alone caused an immediate flight and probing response followed by sustained walking, flying, and probing that took approximately 15 min to return to baseline.
source: In contrast, fictive CO2 alone caused an immediate flight and probing response followed by sustained walking, flying, and probing (Figure 2H, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Video 1) that took approximately 15 min to return to baseline (t1/2 probing = 3.9 min).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Varying the light intensity changed the proportion of mosquitoes responding but not the duration of the response.
source: Varying the light intensity changed the proportion of mosquitoes responding but not the duration of the response (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-D.

claim: The long duration of the response to CO2 is reminiscent of persistent internal states in other organisms.
source: The long duration of the response to CO2 is reminiscent of persistent internal states in other organisms (Asahina et al., 2014; Flavell et al., 2013; Kohatsu et al., 2011; Hindmarsh Sten et al., 2021; Marques et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is an interpretation based on comparison with prior published work on persistent states in other organisms.

claim: Bright light is an arousal signal in mosquitoes.
source: Like CO2, bright light is also an arousal signal in mosquitoes (Araripe et al., 2018) so we asked whether bright light induces a long-lasting behavior state.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: Mosquitoes have weaker visual sensitivity to red wavelengths.
source: Mosquitoes have weaker visual sensitivity to red wavelengths (San Alberto et al., 2021), and we saw no behavioral response to red light (Figure 2E), so we used green light.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published work and experimental data in Figure 2E.

claim: A bright green light stimulus induced a brief response dominated by walking with a half-life of 0.4 min.
source: A bright green light stimulus induced a brief response dominated by walking (t1/2 walking = 0.4 min), much shorter than the response to fictive CO2 (Figure 2I and K).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2I and K.

claim: Mosquitoes possess a second, distinct feeding program for ingestion of flower nectar for energy.
source: While CO2 and heat elicit the blood-feeding program required for females to produce eggs, mosquitoes possess a second, distinct feeding program for ingestion of flower nectar for energy (Jové et al., 2020; Lahondère et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Fictive sugar elicited a response composed largely of probing that was of shorter duration than fictive CO2 with a half-life of 1.5 min.
source: We found that fictive sugar elicited a response composed largely of probing that was of shorter duration than fictive CO2 (t1/2 probing = 1.5 min) (Figure 2J and L).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2J and L.

claim: The heightened probing response seen when heat and fictive CO2 stimuli were presented together was roughly additive with respect to the individual stimuli.
source: We found that the heightened probing response seen when the stimuli were presented together was roughly additive with respect to the individual stimuli (Figure 2M, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2M and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Flying was strongly suppressed when heat and fictive CO2 were presented together.
source: In contrast, flying was strongly suppressed.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2M and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Multimodal integration of host cues biases action selection away from long-range flight and toward probing, a short-range behavior.
source: This demonstrates that multimodal integration of host cues biases action selection away from long-range flight and toward probing, a short-range behavior.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the experimental results shown in Figure 2M and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Probing was suppressed when non-host cues (heat with green light or fictive sugar) were presented together.
source: In contrast to the integration of host cues, probing was suppressed when non-host cues were presented together (Figure 2M, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2M and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The mosquito nervous system uses different computations for the integration of host cues and non-host cues.
source: This demonstrates that the mosquito nervous system uses different computations for the integration of host cues and non-host cues.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the experimental results shown in Figure 2M and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Host seeking in A. aegypti is suppressed after a female takes a blood meal, only returning after she lays eggs several days later.
source: Host seeking in A. aegypti is suppressed after a female takes a blood meal, only returning after she lays eggs several days later (Duvall et al., 2017; Klowden, 1981).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Blood-fed females completely lost their response to fictive CO2 and nearly completely lost their response to heat.
source: We found that blood-fed females completely lost their response to fictive CO2 and nearly completely lost their response to heat (Figure 3A, B, D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A, B, D and E.

claim: Blood-fed females had reduced responses to fictive sugar, but unlike fictive CO2, the response was still detectable.
source: We found that blood-fed females had reduced responses to fictive sugar, but unlike fictive CO2, the response was still detectable (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-E.

claim: Blood-fed females specifically show a complete loss of the persistent state elicited by fictive CO2.
source: This demonstrates that blood-fed females specifically show a complete loss of the persistent state elicited by fictive CO2.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the experimental results shown in Figure 3A, B, D and E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-E.

claim: Male mosquitoes do not seek out hosts to feed on blood.
source: Unlike females, male mosquitoes do not seek out hosts to feed on blood.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about mosquito biology.

claim: Males demonstrate a flight response to CO2.
source: Males do demonstrate a flight response to CO2 (Matthews et al., 2016) and are reported to congregate in the vicinity of humans where they mate with female mosquitoes (Hartberg, 1971).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Males are reported to congregate in the vicinity of humans where they mate with female mosquitoes.
source: Males do demonstrate a flight response to CO2 (Matthews et al., 2016) and are reported to congregate in the vicinity of humans where they mate with female mosquitoes (Hartberg, 1971).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: Male mosquitoes had minimal responses to heat, but substantial flight and walking responses to fictive CO2.
source: We observed that male mosquitoes had minimal responses to heat, but substantial flight and walking responses to fictive CO2 (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C-E.

claim: The response of males to fictive CO2 was brief, decaying rapidly back to baseline with a half-life of 0.4 min.
source: However, the response to fictive CO2 was brief, decaying rapidly back to baseline (t1/2 probing = 0.4 min).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C-E.

claim: The persistence—but not the initial response—to fictive CO2 is specifically regulated in a sexually dimorphic manner.
source: This observation suggests that the persistence—but not the initial response—is specifically regulated in a sexually dimorphic manner.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the experimental results comparing male and female responses to fictive CO2.

claim: Fruitless mutant male mosquitoes gain strong attraction to human odor.
source: We have previously shown that fruitless mutant male mosquitoes gain strong attraction to human odor (Basrur et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published work by the authors.

claim: Fruitless heterozygotes receiving fictive CO2 showed a brief response with a half-life of 0.4 min.
source: fruitless heterozygotes receiving fictive CO2 showed a brief response (t1/2 probing = 0.4 min) (Figure 3G1 and J), similar to the response we saw for wild-type males (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G and J.

claim: Fruitless mutant males receiving fictive CO2 showed a strong and sustained response for minutes after the stimulus with a half-life of 1.7 min.
source: By comparison, fruitless mutant males receiving fictive CO2 showed a strong and sustained response for minutes after the stimulus (t1/2 probing = 1.7 min) (Figure 3H–J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3H-J.

claim: Fruitless is involved in the regulation of the sexual dimorphism of the persistent host-seeking state.
source: This suggests that fruitless is involved in the regulation of the sexual dimorphism of the persistent host-seeking state.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the experimental results shown in Figure 3H-J.

claim: The duration of the sustained response of fruitless mutant males is shorter than in females, suggesting additional sexually dimorphic factors may regulate this internal state.
source: We note that the duration of the sustained response of fruitless mutant males is shorter than in females, suggesting additional sexually dimorphic factors may regulate this internal state.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the experimental results comparing fruitless mutant males to females.

claim: Blood-fed females and males, which do not engage in blood-feeding behavior, lack sustained responses to brief pulses of fictive CO2.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that blood-fed females and males, which do not engage in blood-feeding behavior, lack sustained responses to brief pulses of fictive CO2.
evidence: This claim is a summary of the experimental results shown in Figure 3.

claim: The persistent state is the behavioral mechanism by which the goal of blood feeding is sustained in the female mosquito.
source: This raises the possibility that the persistent state is the behavioral mechanism by which the goal of blood feeding is sustained in the female mosquito.
evidence: This claim is a speculative interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: Motivation consists of two components: increased arousal and directed action toward a goal.
source: Motivation consists of two components: increased arousal and directed action toward a goal.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about motivation.

claim: Fictive CO2 induces a prolonged increase in movement and the probing behavior that immediately precedes blood feeding.
source: We have demonstrated that fictive CO2 induces a prolonged increase in movement and the probing behavior that immediately precedes blood feeding.
evidence: This claim is a summary of the experimental results shown in Figure 2.

claim: CO2 is highly volatile, so mosquitoes likely sense this cue before body heat in naturalistic host-seeking settings.
source: Because CO2 is highly volatile, mosquitoes likely sense this cue before body heat in naturalistic host-seeking settings.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the physical properties of CO2 and knowledge of mosquito behavior.

claim: When heat was presented first followed by fictive CO2, relatively small behavioral responses were evoked.
source: When we presented heat first followed by fictive CO2, relatively small behavioral responses were evoked (Figure 4B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B-C.

claim: When fictive CO2 was presented simultaneously with heat or 15 or 60 s prior to heat, larger walking and probing responses were seen.
source: However, when fictive CO2 was presented simultaneously with heat or 15 or 60 s prior to heat, larger walking and probing responses were seen (Figure 4B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B-C.

claim: Mosquitoes respond most strongly to the naturalistic temporal order of host cues.
source: This suggests that mosquitoes respond most strongly to the naturalistic temporal order of these host cues.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the experimental results shown in Figure 4B-C.

claim: Walking and probing were detectably increased when a fictive CO2 stimulus was presented up to 4 min prior to heat.
source: Compared to heat alone, walking and probing were detectably increased when a fictive CO2 stimulus was presented up to 4 min prior (Figure 4E–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E-F.

claim: Fictive CO2 increases the response to heat for minutes afterward.
source: This demonstrates that in addition to the sustained behavior response, fictive CO2 increases the response to heat for minutes afterward.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the experimental results shown in Figure 4E-F.

claim: ATP in saline has previously been shown to be a highly palatable meal that induces females to engorge in the same manner as blood.
source: We used a solution of ATP in saline, which has previously been shown to be a highly palatable meal that induces females to engorge in the same manner as blood (Galun et al., 1963; Jové et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: When fictive CO2 was presented along with heating of the meal for 10 min, many females fed to repletion.
source: When fictive CO2 was presented along with heating of the meal for 10 min, many females fed to repletion (Figure 4I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: When the order was swapped and females were briefly offered the warm meal prior to fictive CO2, very few females fed.
source: When the order was swapped and females were briefly offered the warm meal prior to fictive CO2, very few females fed (Figure 4I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Mosquitoes feed at the highest rates when they receive a CO2 stimulus prior to heat and taste stimuli.
source: This suggests that mosquitoes feed at the highest rates when they receive a CO2 stimulus prior to heat and taste stimuli.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the experimental results shown in Figure 4I.

claim: When offered the warm meal without fictive CO2, few females fed.
source: When offered the warm meal without fictive CO2, few females fed.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4J.

claim: Fictive CO2 was able to potentiate feeding when presented up to 14 min prior to heating of the blood meal mimic.
source: Indeed, fictive CO2 was able to potentiate feeding when presented up to 14 min prior to heating of the blood meal mimic (Figure 4J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4J.

claim: The persistent state reflects the amount of time a mosquito will pursue a host in a naturalistic setting before halting the search if it appears that the host is no longer nearby.
source: We speculate that this reflects the amount of time a mosquito will pursue a host in a naturalistic setting before halting the search if it appears that the host is no longer nearby.
evidence: This claim is a speculative interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: Mosquito behavior fell into four major states termed rest, global search, local search, and engorge.
source: This embedding revealed that mosquito behavior fell into four major states that we termed rest, global search, local search, and engorge (Figure 4K, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by tSNE analysis shown in Figure 4K and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The engorge state was greatly enriched in mosquitoes that were categorized as fed.
source: As expected, the engorge state was greatly enriched in mosquitoes that were categorized as fed, demonstrating that this method is effective at identifying longer-timescale behavior states (Figure 4L).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4L.

claim: Fed and unfed mosquitoes showed similar amounts of global search pre-heat but greater levels of local search for those that would later feed.
source: We found that fed and unfed mosquitoes showed similar amounts of global search pre-heat but greater levels of local search for those that would later feed (Figure 4M).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4M.

claim: A classifier trained on the proportion of time mosquitoes spent in each behavior for 2 min after the light stimulus could predict which mosquitoes would later feed with above-chance accuracy.
source: A classifier trained on the proportion of time mosquitoes spent in each behavior for 2 min after the light stimulus could predict which mosquitoes would later feed with above-chance accuracy (Figure 4N).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4N.

claim: The behavior state that individual mosquitoes enter in response to fictive CO2 reflects the likelihood of response to future sensory cues.
source: Thus, the behavior state that individual mosquitoes enter in response to fictive CO2 reflects the likelihood of response to future sensory cues.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the experimental results shown in Figure 4N.

claim: Optogenetic activation of CO2 sensory neurons induced a long-lasting behavior state change.
source: These experiments demonstrated that optogenetic activation of CO2 sensory neurons induced a long-lasting behavior state change (Figure 4O).
evidence: This claim is a summary of the experimental results shown throughout the manuscript.

claim: During the persistent state, mosquitoes had heightened responses to heat and were more likely to feed on a blood meal mimic even if encountered minutes after the CO2 stimulus.
source: During this time mosquitoes had heightened responses to heat and were more likely to feed on a blood meal mimic even if encountered minutes after the CO2 stimulus.
evidence: This claim is a summary of the experimental results shown in Figure 4.

claim: Integration of sensory information over time allows the nervous system to optimize decision making for a particular goal.
source: Integration of sensory information over time allows the nervous system to optimize decision making for a particular goal (Körding, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: Laboratory studies have found behavior responses altered for as long as a few seconds after encountering CO2 in mosquitoes and other olfactory stimuli in Drosophila.
source: Laboratory studies have found behavior responses altered for as long as a few seconds after encountering CO2 in mosquitoes and other olfactory stimuli in Drosophila (Alvarez-Salvado et al., 2018; Dekker and Cardé, 2011; Demir et al., 2020; Pang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Modelling suggests that integration over long timescales can maximize the information about the location of an olfactory stimulus.
source: Although this timescale of sensory integration is sufficient for upwind tracking, modelling suggests that integration over long timescales can maximize the information about the location of an olfactory stimulus (Vergassola et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: Mosquitoes integrate olfactory, heat, and taste stimuli for at least 14 min, much longer than previously assumed.
source: Here, we show that mosquitoes integrate olfactory, heat, and taste stimuli for at least 14 min, much longer than previously assumed.
evidence: This claim is a summary of the experimental results shown in Figure 4.

claim: The internal state does not require constant flight behavior or a constant air flow stimulus, demonstrating that it is maintained by an internal mechanism rather than continuous sensory or reafferent stimuli.
source: Importantly, our results show that this internal state does not require constant flight behavior or a constant air flow stimulus, demonstrating that it is maintained by an internal mechanism rather than continuous sensory or reafferent stimuli.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the experimental results showing persistent behavior without continuous stimulation.

claim: CO2 sensory neurons in A. aegypti show an accurate readout of CO2 levels over a large concentration range.
source: However, it is extensively documented in A. aegypti that CO2 sensory neurons show an accurate readout of CO2 levels over a large concentration range (Grant and O'Connell, 2007; Grant et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: CO2 sensory neurons do not show adaptation or prolonged activity.
source: These neurons do not show adaptation or prolonged activity (Grant et al., 1995) and have similar responses in males and females (Grant and O'Connell, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: CO2 sensory neurons have similar responses in males and females.
source: These neurons do not show adaptation or prolonged activity (Grant et al., 1995) and have similar responses in males and females (Grant and O'Connell, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: In mice, circuits originating in the central amygdala promote pursuit and attack during cricket hunting.
source: In mice, circuits originating in the central amygdala promote pursuit and attack during cricket hunting (Han et al., 2017), but these behaviors appear time-locked to optogenetic activation and a circuit controlling hunting persistence has not been identified.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: Mosquito host seeking shares some characteristics with other social and feeding states.
source: Mosquito host seeking shares some characteristics with other social and feeding states (Asahina et al., 2014; Flavell et al., 2013; Kohatsu et al., 2011; Hindmarsh Sten et al., 2021; Marques et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: In response to female sensory cues or stimulation of a subset of fruitless neurons, male flies enter a state of increased courtship behaviors and lower thresholds for sensory cues from females.
